correctness.rationale: For each k>=2 and positive real gaps, enumerating the omitted report gives weights P/g_1, P/g_k, and P(1/g_j+1/g_{j+1}); the sum is 2P sum 1/g_i. The corresponding cost numerator is P[k+1+sum min(g_i,g_{i+1})/max(g_i,g_{i+1})]. Pigeonhole and the triangle inequality prove OPT=min g. Choosing a shortest gap and an adjacent one yields R<=((2k-1)+u)/(2(1+u))<k-1/2, while gaps (1,T,...,T) tend to that supremum. Every omission has positive probability, yielding the exact equality-at-one criterion. 21,844 standalone exact-rational finite checks from VERIFY.py matched the proof but are not treated as proof by enumeration.

value.rationale: The n=k+1 case is the smallest population with a nonzero possibility of unserved demand and a natural parameter endpoint of facility-location mechanisms. Its exact welfare ratio k-1/2 is strictly smaller than the cited unrestricted 2k, for every k, with 3-facility ratio 5/2 at the first nontrivial n=4. The characterization of all welfare-optimal nonuniform profiles by isolated long gaps exposes a structural dependence on gap adjacency, not merely an isolated numerical instance. The result supports precise small-market benchmarking; it does not purport to solve larger-population incentive or welfare questions.
